claims.text: Native document fonts and layout can depend on the receiving environment.
Camelot sought practical visual-document exchange using existing print technology.
PDF represents composed pages using text, vector graphics and images; font inclusion is conditional.
Acrobat arrived in 1993; Reader became free with Acrobat 2.0 in 1994.
Free receiving can increase the usefulness of paid creation and workflow tools.
Appearance alone does not establish correct reading order.
Version, omitted context and truth require more than visual fidelity.
A portable context record might help applicability judgments.
A familiar receiving format can feel reassuring and reduce negotiation about receiving a document.
claims.status: Achim’s situated experience and design hypothesis; no public-trust measurement

claims.text: Cryptographic signature validation concerns certificate trust and integrity of signed content; a visual mark alone provides no such check.
claims.status: supported with mechanism/software/trust and later-change caveats
claims.qualification: Does not establish factual truth, universal identity assurance, immutability or legal equivalence.

claims.text: Font substitution/reflow and missing glyphs or encoding/mapping failures are distinct failure modes.
claims.qualification: Explicit boxes, not an assertion that Courier lacks umlauts. Original specimen remains semantic text. PDF is not immune to missing resources or extraction failures.

claims.text: Search context may help assess applicability; AI-mediated context and private contributions returning to shared knowledge are separate questions.
